Count Rouvaloff stared at him in surprise for several moments. Once he realized that he was serious, he wrote an address on a piece of paper, added his initials, and passed it across the table.

'Scotland Yard would pay a great deal for this address, my dear fellow.'

'They won't get it,' Lord Arthur replied with a laugh. He warmly shook the young Russian's hand, hurried downstairs, read the paper, and instructed his coachman to take him to Soho Square.

There he sent the coachman away and walked down Greek Street until he reached Bayle's Court. Passing beneath an archway, he entered a strange little dead end that seemed to house a French laundry. Clotheslines formed a web between the buildings, and white linen fluttered in the morning air. He walked to the far end and knocked at a small green house. While he waited, every window filled with indistinct faces peering out. Eventually a rather rough-looking foreigner opened the door and asked in very poor English what he wanted. Lord Arthur handed over Count Rouvaloff's note. The man read it, bowed, and led him into a shabby front sitting room on the ground floor. A few moments later, Herr Winckelkopf, as he was known in England, bustled in with a badly wine-stained napkin around his neck and a fork in his left hand.

'Count Rouvaloff has introduced me to you,' Lord Arthur said, bowing. 'I'd like a short business discussion. My name is Smith—Mr. Robert Smith—and I want you to provide me with an exploding clock.'

'Delighted to meet you, Lord Arthur,' the friendly little German said, laughing. 'Don't look so frightened. Knowing everyone is part of my business. I remember seeing you one evening at Lady Windermere's. I hope she's well. Will you join me while I finish breakfast? There's an excellent pâté, and my friends kindly tell me that my Rhine wine is better than anything at the German Embassy.' Before Lord Arthur recovered from the surprise of being recognized, he was seated in the back room. He sipped delicious Marcobrünner from a pale yellow wineglass bearing the Imperial monogram and chatted warmly with the famous conspirator.

'Exploding clocks,' Herr Winckelkopf said, 'aren't particularly suitable for sending abroad. Even if they get through Customs, the trains are so unreliable that the clocks generally explode before arriving where they're supposed to go.'

Mr. Bennet said almost nothing throughout dinner. Once the servants had departed, however, he judged it time to engage his visitor in conversation, and chose a topic upon which he expected him to excel. He remarked on Mr. Collins's apparent good fortune in his patroness: Lady Catherine de Bourgh's attention to his wishes and concern for his comfort seemed extraordinary. No subject could have been better selected. Mr. Collins became eloquent in her commendation, his manner assuming even more than its customary gravity. With an air of immense importance, he declared that never had he encountered such conduct in anyone of rank, such graciousness and condescension as Lady Catherine had shown him. She had generously approved both sermons he had so far enjoyed the honour of delivering in her presence. Twice she had invited him to dine at Rosings, and only the preceding Saturday had summoned him to complete her evening table of quadrille. He knew many people considered her proud, but he himself had witnessed nothing except kindness. She invariably addressed him as she would any other gentleman. She raised no objection to his entering neighbourhood society, or occasionally leaving his parish for a week or two to visit his family. She had even stooped to recommend that he marry at the earliest opportunity, so long as he chose wisely. Once she had honoured his modest parsonage with a visit, approved every alteration he had undertaken, and graciously proposed improvements of her own: shelves in the upstairs closets.

'All very proper and courteous, I am sure,' Mrs. Bennet said. 'She must be a most agreeable woman. What a pity more great ladies do not resemble her. Is her home near yours, sir?'

'The garden containing my humble dwelling is divided from Rosings Park, her ladyship's residence, by a lane alone.'

'I believe you mentioned that she is widowed? Does she have children?'

'One daughter only, heir to Rosings and to a very considerable estate.'

'Ah!' Mrs. Bennet exclaimed, shaking her head. 'Then she has more advantages than many girls. What sort of young lady is she? Is she pretty?'

'She is exceedingly charming. Lady Catherine herself assures me that in genuine beauty Miss de Bourgh surpasses the loveliest women, for something in her features unmistakably denotes a young lady of distinguished ancestry.'

Besides, few people other than sailors can tie this knot, and it is particularly associated with Maltese seamen. I found the ribbon at the base of the lightning rod. It could not have belonged to either victim. Now, even if my inference is wrong and the Frenchman is not a sailor on a Maltese ship, the wording of my advertisement can do no harm. He will simply assume that some circumstance misled me and will not bother investigating it. If I am right, though, we gain a substantial advantage. Although innocent of the murders, the Frenchman knows about them and will naturally hesitate to answer the advertisement and claim the orangutan. He will reason as follows: 'I am innocent and poor. My orangutan is extremely valuable—a fortune to someone in my position. Why sacrifice it because of groundless fears? I can recover it now. It was found in the Bois de Boulogne, far from the scene of the massacre. Who would imagine an animal responsible for that? The police are baffled; they have found no clue at all. Even if they trace the creature, they cannot prove I knew about the murders, or make me guilty merely because I knew. Above all, someone knows who I am. The advertiser identifies me as the owner, and I don't know how much else he knows. If I refuse to claim valuable property known to belong to me, I shall at least make the animal look suspicious. Drawing attention to either of us is against my interests. I'll answer the notice, retrieve the orangutan, and hide it until the affair has blown over.'"

Just then we heard footsteps on the stairs.

"Keep your pistols ready," Dupin said, "but don't display or use them unless I signal you."

The front door had been left open. Our visitor had entered without ringing and climbed several steps, but now appeared to hesitate. Soon we heard him going down again. Dupin moved swiftly toward the door, only for the footsteps to turn upward once more. This time the visitor did not retreat. He came up decisively and knocked at our room.

"Come in," Dupin called in a warm, cheerful voice.

A man entered, plainly a sailor: tall, broad, and muscular, with a reckless expression that was not entirely unattractive.
